records.source: וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט עֹ֥שֶׁר וְכָב֖וֹד לָרֹ֑ב וַיִּתְחַתֵּ֖ן לְאַחְאָֽב׃
records.gloss: And was to Jehoshaphat riches and honor in abundance, and he made himself [a] son-in-law to Ahab.
pieces: Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab.

L.1: And Jehoshaphat had riches and honor in abundance, and he allied himself by marriage with Ahab.

R.1: Jehoshaphat was very rich and highly honored. He also made an alliance with Ahab through a marriage between their families.

decisions.choice: Chronicles' own opening to the story told in 1 Kings 22:1-35
decisions.reason: This chapter retells 1 Kings 22:1-35, the campaign against Ramoth-gilead and the death of Ahab, mostly in the same words. Chronicles leaves out 1 Kings 22:1 (three years without war between Aram and Israel) and opens instead with this verse, which has no parallel in Kings. It repeats Jehoshaphat's riches and honor from 17:5 and adds his marriage alliance with Ahab. The notes on each verse below name where the Hebrew differs from Kings.

decisions.choice: made himself a son-in-law to Ahab: joined his royal house to Ahab's by a marriage
decisions.reason: The verb means to become related by marriage (Deuteronomy 7:3; 1 Kings 3:1). The marriage was between their children: Jehoshaphat's son Jehoram married Ahab's daughter Athaliah (21:6; 22:2; 2 Kings 8:18, 26). Marriages between royal houses sealed alliances between kingdoms.

decisions.choice: riches and honor ... and he allied himself: the alliance set beside his strength
decisions.reason: The verse puts the two facts side by side. After chapter 17 has shown how Yahweh made Jehoshaphat strong and rich (17:5), the alliance with Ahab may be meant to look needless. A prophet later rebukes him for helping Ahab (19:2). The Hebrew only says "and", so the contrast is implied, not stated.

decisions.choice: through a marriage between their families
decisions.reason: Readable says that the alliance was made by a marriage between the two royal families (m2), since "made himself a son-in-law" would suggest that Jehoshaphat himself married into Ahab's family.

records.heading: Micaiah prophesies against Ahab

records.source: וַיֵּרֶד֩ לְקֵ֨ץ שָׁנִ֤ים אֶל־אַחְאָב֙ לְשֹׁ֣מְר֔וֹן וַיִּֽזְבַּֽח־ל֨וֹ אַחְאָ֜ב צֹ֤אן וּבָקָר֙ לָרֹ֔ב וְלָעָ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֣ר עִמּ֑וֹ וַיְסִיתֵ֕הוּ לַעֲל֖וֹת אֶל־רָמ֥וֹת גִּלְעָֽד׃
records.gloss: And he went down at [the] end of years to Ahab to Samaria, and slaughtered for him Ahab sheep and cattle in abundance, and for the people who [were] with him, and he enticed him to go up against Ramoth-gilead.
pieces: Some years later he went down to visit Ahab in Samaria. Ahab slaughtered sheep and cattle in great numbers for him and for the people who were with him, and he urged him to go up against Ramoth-gilead.

L.2: And at [the] end of [some] years he went down to Ahab, to Samaria. And Ahab slaughtered sheep and cattle in abundance for him and for the people who [were] with him, and he enticed him to go up against Ramoth-gilead.

R.2: Some years later, Jehoshaphat went to visit Ahab in the city of Samaria. Ahab killed a great many sheep and cattle to hold a feast for him and for the people with him. And Ahab urged Jehoshaphat to join him in attacking the city of Ramoth-gilead.

decisions.choice: the visit of 1 Kings 22:2, told with a feast and with Ahab's persuasion
decisions.reason: 1 Kings 22:2 says that "in the third year" Jehoshaphat went down to the king of Israel. Chronicles says "at the end of years", names Ahab and Samaria, and adds the feast Ahab gave and his urging Jehoshaphat to join the war. It leaves out 1 Kings 22:3, where the king of Israel tells his officials that Ramoth-gilead belongs to Israel and is still held by the king of Aram. In Chronicles the war is Ahab's plan, and Jehoshaphat is drawn into it.

decisions.choice: enticed: urged, drew him on, often toward harm
decisions.reason: The verb means to urge or lure someone, usually toward something wrong or harmful (Deuteronomy 13:7; 1 Chronicles 21:1). Ahab wins Jehoshaphat over with lavish hospitality. The same verb comes back in verse 31, where God draws the enemy chariots away from Jehoshaphat.

decisions.choice: slaughtered sheep and cattle: a great feast of welcome
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to sacrifice, but it is also used of killing animals for a feast (1 Kings 1:9, 19). Here it is a royal banquet for Jehoshaphat and all his company, a sign of honor that also served Ahab's purpose.

decisions.choice: Ramoth-gilead: an Israelite town east of the Jordan held by Aram
decisions.reason: Ramoth in Gilead lay east of the Jordan, in the territory of Gad. It was one of the cities of refuge (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8). According to 1 Kings 22:3 it belonged to Israel but was in the hands of the king of Aram.

decisions.choice: went down: traveled from Jerusalem north to Samaria
decisions.reason: Jerusalem stands high in the hill country, so a journey away from it is spoken of as going down, as in 1 Kings 22:2. Samaria was Ahab's capital.

decisions.choice: went down to visit; to hold a feast; to join him in attacking
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "to visit", as 1 Kings 22:2 does, to make clear this was a royal visit. Readable also says what the slaughter was for (m3), names the two kings where "he" and "him" would be unclear, and adds "the city of" to the place names.

records.source: וַיֹּ֜אמֶר אַחְאָ֣ב מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֶל־יְהֽוֹשָׁפָט֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה הֲתֵלֵ֥ךְ עִמִּ֖י רָמֹ֣ת גִּלְעָ֑ד וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ כָּמ֤וֹנִי כָמ֨וֹךָ֙ וּכְעַמְּךָ֣ עַמִּ֔י וְעִמְּךָ֖ בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said Ahab king of Israel to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, will you go with me [to] Ramoth-gilead? And he said to him, as me as you, and as your people my people, and with you in the battle.
pieces: Ahab king of Israel asked Jehoshaphat king of Judah, "Will you come with me to Ramoth-gilead?" He replied, "I am as you are, and my troops are as your troops. We will be with you in the battle."

L.3: And Ahab king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, "Will you go with me [to] Ramoth-gilead?" And he said to him, "As I [am], so [are] you; and as your people, so my people; and [we will be] with you in the battle."

R.3: Ahab king of Israel asked Jehoshaphat king of Judah, "Will you join me in attacking Ramoth-gilead?" Jehoshaphat told him, "I am with you all the way. My army is yours to command. We will go into battle with you."

decisions.choice: the request and answer of 1 Kings 22:4, with three differences
decisions.reason: Chronicles names Ahab and gives both kings their titles, where 1 Kings 22:4 has only "he said to Jehoshaphat". The question lacks "to battle". Jehoshaphat's answer turns one pair around ("as your people, so my people"), leaves out the horses, and ends with a promise of its own: "and with you in the battle".

decisions.choice: as I am, so are you ...: I am fully with you; all I have is at your disposal
decisions.reason: Jehoshaphat answers with a set saying of alliance. He puts himself and his army on the same footing as Ahab's, and then says it plainly: he will be with Ahab in the battle, fighting alongside him as one force.

decisions.choice: your people ... my people: your army ... my army
decisions.reason: Here "people" means the fighting men a king leads into battle, as often in these books.

decisions.choice: troops / army
decisions.reason: The army sense of "people" (m3): Literal keeps "people", Balanced says "troops" and Readable "army", as in these books generally.

decisions.choice: [we will be] with you / We will be with you
decisions.reason: The last clause has no verb. Literal brackets the words English needs; Balanced and Readable supply them. Readable also says what the saying means (m2), as in 1 Kings 22:4, and names Jehoshaphat where the Hebrew has "he".

records.source: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל דְּרָשׁ־נָ֥א כַיּ֖וֹם אֶת־דְּבַ֥ר יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said Jehoshaphat to [the] king of Israel, seek please as the day the word of Yahweh.
pieces: But Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "First, please seek the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."

L.4: And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Please inquire today for the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."

R.4: But Jehoshaphat also said to the king of Israel, "First, please ask {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says."

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:5
decisions.reason: This verse is word for word the same as 1 Kings 22:5, and its wording here is the same.

decisions.choice: seek the word of Yahweh: ask a prophet for Yahweh's answer before going to war
decisions.reason: Kings asked God before a battle whether to go and whether they would win, usually through a prophet or a priest (1 Samuel 23:2-4; 30:7-8). Jehoshaphat will not set out until this has been done.

decisions.choice: as the day: first, now, before anything else
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean "today" or "at once". Here it asks that the inquiry be made now, before they march.

decisions.choice: First
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "first" for the sense of m3; Literal keeps "today".

records.source: וַיִּקְבֹּ֨ץ מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֥ל אֶֽת־הַנְּבִאִים֮ אַרְבַּ֣ע מֵא֣וֹת אִישׁ֒ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֗ם הֲנֵלֵ֞ךְ אֶל־רָמֹ֥ת גִּלְעָ֛ד לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה אִם־אֶחְדָּ֑ל וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ עֲלֵ֔ה וְיִתֵּ֥ן הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים בְּיַ֥ד הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And gathered [the] king of Israel the prophets, four hundred man, and said to them, shall we go against Ramoth-gilead for battle, or shall I refrain? And they said, go up, and will give the God into [the] hand of the king.
pieces: So the king of Israel gathered the prophets, four hundred men, and asked them, "Shall we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I hold back?" "Go up," they said, "for God will give it into the king's hand."

L.5: And the king of Israel gathered the prophets, four hundred men, and said to them, "Shall we go against Ramoth-gilead for battle, or shall I refrain?" And they said, "Go up, and God will give [it] into the hand of the king."

R.5: So the king of Israel called together four hundred prophets. He asked them, "Should we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or not?" They answered, "Go! God will help you capture it, Your Majesty."

decisions.choice: "God" where 1 Kings 22:6 has "the Lord"
decisions.reason: In 1 Kings 22:6 the prophets answer with the title "the Lord" (Adonai). Chronicles has "God" (with the article, "the God"), a word it often uses where Samuel and Kings have the divine name or a title. The prophets use the name Yahweh in verses 10-11, as in Kings. Chronicles also says "four hundred men" where Kings has "about four hundred", and the king asks "shall we go" where Kings has "shall I go".

decisions.choice: the prophets: a large group of court prophets
decisions.reason: These four hundred are prophets attached to Ahab's court. They speak in the name of Yahweh (verses 10-11, 23), but Jehoshaphat is not satisfied with them (verse 6).

decisions.choice: will give into the hand of the king: an answer that does not name what is given
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has no object: "will give into the hand of the king". The natural sense is that the city will be given to Ahab. The answer is also loose enough to be fulfilled in another way, since it does not say which king or what will be given; verses 18-22 show the promise was a deception.

decisions.choice: give into the hand of: give victory over, let capture
decisions.reason: To give something into someone's hand is to put it in their power.

decisions.choice: shall we go ... or shall I refrain?: "we" and "I" in one question
decisions.reason: The king first speaks for both kings ("we"), then of himself ("I"). The question is still the one decision: whether the campaign goes ahead.

decisions.choice: it
decisions.reason: Balanced supplies "it", the city, as the natural object (m3). Literal brackets the word.

decisions.choice: help you capture it, Your Majesty
decisions.reason: Readable says what "give into the hand" means (m4) and turns "the king" into a direct address, since the prophets are speaking to him.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יְה֣וֹשָׁפָ֔ט הַאֵ֨ין פֹּ֥ה נָבִ֛יא לַיהוָ֖ה ע֑וֹד וְנִדְרְשָׁ֖ה מֵאֹתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And said Jehoshaphat, is there not here a prophet of Yahweh still, and we may inquire of him?
pieces: But Jehoshaphat said, "Is there no other prophet of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} here whom we can ask?"

L.6: And Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not here still a prophet of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, that we may inquire of him?"

R.6: But Jehoshaphat asked, "Is there not another prophet of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} here? We should ask him too."

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:7
decisions.reason: This verse matches 1 Kings 22:7 except for a small difference in how one word is written, which does not change the sense. Its wording here is the same as there.

decisions.choice: is there not still here a prophet of Yahweh?: is there no other prophet besides these?
decisions.reason: "Still" means "besides" or "in addition". Jehoshaphat does not deny that the four hundred are prophets, but he wants another voice. The question suggests that he does not trust their quick agreement.

decisions.choice: other / another
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable express "still" as "other" (m2).

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל׀אֶֽל־יְהוֹשָׁפָ֡ט ע֣וֹד אִישׁ־אֶחָ֡ד לִדְרוֹשׁ֩ אֶת־יְהוָ֨ה מֵֽאֹת֜וֹ וַאֲנִ֣י שְׂנֵאתִ֗יהוּ כִּֽי־אֵ֠ינֶנּוּ מִתְנַבֵּ֨א עָלַ֤י לְטוֹבָה֙ כִּ֣י כָל־יָמָ֣יו לְרָעָ֔ה ה֖וּא מִיכָ֣יְהוּ בֶן־יִמְלָ֑א וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יְה֣וֹשָׁפָ֔ט אַל־יֹאמַ֥ר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ כֵּֽן׃
records.gloss: And said [the] king of Israel to Jehoshaphat, still [there is] one man to inquire of Yahweh from him, and I hate him, for he [is] not prophesying concerning me for good, but all his days for evil; he [is] Micaiah son of Imlah. And said Jehoshaphat, not let say the king so.
pieces: The king of Israel answered Jehoshaphat, "There is still one man through whom we could inquire of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him, for his prophecies about me are never good, but always bad." Jehoshaphat said, "Let the king not speak like that."

L.7: And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "[There is] still one man by whom to inquire of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, but I hate him, for he does not prophesy concerning me for good, but all his days for evil: he [is] Micaiah son of Imlah." And Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so."

R.7: The king of Israel answered Jehoshaphat, "There is one more man we could ask to find out what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says. But I hate him. He never says anything good about me. He always predicts trouble for me. His name is Micaiah son of Imlah." Jehoshaphat said, "Your Majesty, you should not say that."

decisions.choice: "all his days for evil" where 1 Kings 22:8 has "but evil"
decisions.reason: Chronicles sharpens Ahab's complaint: Micaiah prophesies not for good "but all his days for evil", that is, always harm. It also adds "he is" before Micaiah's name. Otherwise the verse is the same as 1 Kings 22:8.

decisions.choice: good ... evil: good fortune ... disaster
decisions.reason: "Good" and "evil" here are what the prophecies promise: success or trouble. Ahab complains that Micaiah only ever announces harm for him.

decisions.choice: Micaiah son of Imlah: a prophet of Yahweh known only from this story
decisions.reason: His name means "Who is like Yahweh?" He is not the Micah of the book of Micah, who lived over a century later. Elijah is not mentioned in this chapter.

decisions.choice: let not the king say so: a polite rebuke
decisions.reason: Jehoshaphat speaks of Ahab in the third person, as was polite toward a king. He objects to Ahab's hatred for a prophet of Yahweh, or to the idea that a prophet speaks only to please.

decisions.choice: bad / trouble; always
decisions.reason: Balanced says "bad" and Readable "trouble" for the sense of "evil" here (m2); Literal keeps "evil". Balanced and Readable say "always" for "all his days" (m1).

decisions.choice: Your Majesty, you should not say that
decisions.reason: Readable turns the polite third person (m4) into a direct address.

records.source: וַיִּקְרָא֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶל־סָרִ֖יס אֶחָ֑ד וַיֹּ֕אמֶר מַהֵ֖ר מִיכָ֥יְהוּ בֶן־יִמְלָֽא׃
records.gloss: And called [the] king of Israel to one official, and said, hurry Micaiah son of Imlah.
pieces: So the king of Israel called one of his court officials and said, "Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once."

L.8: And the king of Israel called to one official and said, "Hurry [to bring] Micaiah son of Imlah."

R.8: So the king of Israel sent for one of his officials. He told him, "Go and get Micaiah son of Imlah. Hurry!"

decisions.choice: the same order as 1 Kings 22:9
decisions.reason: The verse matches 1 Kings 22:9. The command "hurry" has a slightly different form there; the sense is the same, and so is the wording here.

decisions.choice: official: a court officer
decisions.reason: The word can mean a eunuch, but it is also the ordinary word for a high officer at a royal court, which is the sense here; nothing in the story turns on whether he was a eunuch.

decisions.choice: hurry Micaiah: bring Micaiah quickly
decisions.reason: The verb "hurry" takes Micaiah as its object: "make Micaiah come quickly".

decisions.choice: official
decisions.reason: Every level says "official" (m2). Literal may say "eunuch" where that sense matters; here it does not.

records.source: וּמֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֡ל וִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֡ה יוֹשְׁבִים֩ אִ֨ישׁ עַל־כִּסְא֜וֹ מְלֻבָּשִׁ֤ים בְּגָדִים֙ וְיֹשְׁבִ֣ים בְּגֹ֔רֶן פֶּ֖תַח שַׁ֣עַר שֹׁמְר֑וֹן וְכָל־הַ֨נְּבִיאִ֔ים מִֽתְנַבְּאִ֖ים לִפְנֵיהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And [the] king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah [were] sitting each on his throne, clothed [in] garments, and [they were] sitting at [the] threshing floor [at the] entrance of [the] gate of Samaria; and all the prophets [were] prophesying before them.
pieces: Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, dressed in their royal robes. They were sitting at the threshing floor at the entrance to the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying in front of them.

L.9: And the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah [were] sitting each on his throne, clothed in robes, and [they were] sitting at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria; and all the prophets [were] prophesying before them.

R.9: The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah sat on their thrones in their royal robes. They were at the threshing floor by the entrance to the city gate of Samaria. All the prophets were there in front of them, prophesying.

decisions.choice: "sitting" said twice, where 1 Kings 22:10 has it once
decisions.reason: Chronicles repeats "and sitting" before "at the threshing floor". The repetition makes clear that the thrones stood at the threshing floor; the scene is the same as in 1 Kings 22:10.

decisions.choice: clothed in garments: wearing royal robes
decisions.reason: "Garments" here are the formal robes of kings seated in state. The scene is a public royal assembly.

decisions.choice: the threshing floor at the gate of Samaria: a broad open space outside the city gate
decisions.reason: A threshing floor was a flat, open area of hard ground. One by the city gate made room for the two kings' thrones and the crowd of four hundred prophets. The gate was the place for public business and judgment.

decisions.choice: prophesying: speaking as prophets, perhaps with ecstatic behavior
decisions.reason: The verb form can describe a prophet's words or the excited behavior that sometimes went with prophecy (1 Samuel 10:5-6; 1 Kings 18:29). Here the next verses show both actions and words.

decisions.choice: royal robes
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "royal" to show what kind of robes these were (m2).

records.source: וַיַּ֥עַשׂ ל֛וֹ צִדְקִיָּ֥הוּ בֶֽן־כְּנַעֲנָ֖ה קַרְנֵ֣י בַרְזֶ֑לוַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה בְּאֵ֛לֶּה תְּנַגַּ֥ח אֶת־אֲרָ֖ם עַד־כַּלּוֹתָֽם׃
records.gloss: And made for himself Zedekiah son of Chenaanah horns of iron, and said, thus says Yahweh, with these you will gore Aram until finishing them.
pieces: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made himself iron horns, and he said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: 'With these you will gore the Arameans until they are destroyed.'"

L.10: And Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: 'With these you will gore Aram until they are finished.'"

R.10: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made some horns out of iron. He said, "This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: 'With horns like these you will gore the Arameans and wipe them out.'"

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:11
decisions.reason: The verse matches 1 Kings 22:11. Zedekiah's name is spelled with a longer ending here, and one verb form differs slightly; neither changes the sense, and the wording is the same as there.

decisions.choice: horns of iron: a sign acted out by the prophet
decisions.reason: Prophets sometimes acted out their message (1 Kings 11:29-31; 2 Kings 13:15-19). The horn of a bull stands for strength and conquest (Deuteronomy 33:17). With iron horns Zedekiah pictures the king as a bull goring Aram to death.

decisions.choice: made: had made, before the scene
decisions.reason: The horns were most likely made before the assembly at the gate, and Zedekiah now shows them; the verb does not require that he made them on the spot.

decisions.choice: Aram: the Aramean people and army
decisions.reason: The country's name stands for its people and army, as the plural "them" at the end shows.

decisions.choice: The LORD says this / This is what the LORD says
decisions.reason: The messenger formula "thus says Yahweh" has one wording at each level in these books. Balanced and Readable name the Arameans (m4).

records.source: וְכָל־הַ֨נְּבִאִ֔ים נִבְּאִ֥ים כֵּ֖ן לֵאמֹ֑ר עֲלֵ֞ה רָמֹ֤ת גִּלְעָד֙ וְהַצְלַ֔ח וְנָתַ֥ן יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַ֥ד הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And all the prophets [were] prophesying so, saying, go up [to] Ramoth-gilead and succeed, and will give Yahweh [it] into [the] hand of the king.
pieces: All the prophets were prophesying the same thing: "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and be victorious. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will give it into the king's hand."

L.11: And all the prophets [were] prophesying so, saying, "Go up [to] Ramoth-gilead and succeed, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will give [it] into the hand of the king."

R.11: All the other prophets were saying the same thing: "Attack Ramoth-gilead and win the battle! {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will help you capture it, Your Majesty."

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:12
decisions.reason: This verse is word for word the same as 1 Kings 22:12, and its wording here is the same.

decisions.choice: succeed: prosper, win
decisions.reason: The verb means to succeed or prosper; in a battle it means victory. Micaiah repeats the words in verse 14.

decisions.choice: will give into the hand of the king: as in verse 5, now with the divine name
decisions.reason: This time the prophets use the name Yahweh, where in verse 5 they said "God". As in verse 5 the Hebrew leaves the object unstated.

decisions.choice: help you capture it, Your Majesty
decisions.reason: As in verse 5.

records.source: וְהַמַּלְאָ֞ךְ אֲשֶׁר־הָלַ֣ךְ׀לִקְרֹ֣א לְמִיכָ֗יְהוּ דִּבֶּ֤ר אֵלָיו֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר הִנֵּ֞ה דִּבְרֵ֧י הַנְּבִאִ֛ים פֶּֽה־אֶחָ֥ד ט֖וֹב אֶל־הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וִֽיהִי־נָ֧א דְבָרְךָ֛ כְּאַחַ֥ד מֵהֶ֖ם וְדִבַּ֥רְתָּ טּֽוֹב׃
records.gloss: And the messenger who had gone to call Micaiah spoke to him, saying, look, [the] words of the prophets [are with] one mouth good to the king; and let be please your word like one of them, and you will speak good.
pieces: The messenger who had gone to call Micaiah said to him, "Listen, the prophets are all speaking with one voice, and what they say is good for the king. Please let your word be like one of theirs, and speak favorably."

L.12: And the messenger who had gone to call Micaiah spoke to him, saying, "Look, the words of the prophets [are] one mouth, good to the king. So let your word, please, be like one of them, and speak good."

R.12: The messenger who went to get Micaiah said to him, "Listen! All the other prophets agree. They are all promising the king success. Please say the same thing they are saying. Give him a good message."

decisions.choice: small differences from 1 Kings 22:13
decisions.reason: Chronicles lacks "please" after "look", joins the request with "and", and says "like one of them" where Kings has "like the word of one of them". The sense is the same as in 1 Kings 22:13.

decisions.choice: one mouth: with one voice, in full agreement
decisions.reason: "One mouth" means that the prophets all say the same thing.

decisions.choice: good: favorable, promising success
decisions.reason: As in verse 7, "good" is a message of success for the king. The messenger presses Micaiah to agree with the others.

decisions.choice: speaking with one voice / all agree
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the English idiom closest to "one mouth"; Readable says what it means (m2).

records.source: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר מִיכָ֑יְהוּ חַי־יְהוָ֕ה כִּ֛י אֶת־אֲשֶׁר־יֹאמַ֥ר אֱלֹהַ֖י אֹת֥וֹ אֲדַבֵּֽר׃
records.gloss: And said Micaiah, [by the] life of Yahweh, that what will say my God, it I will speak.
pieces: But Micaiah said, "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, whatever my God says is what I will speak."

L.13: And Micaiah said, "[As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, what my God says, that I will speak."

R.13: But Micaiah said, "I promise, as surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, I will say only what my God tells me to say."

decisions.choice: "my God" where 1 Kings 22:14 has "Yahweh ... to me"
decisions.reason: In 1 Kings 22:14 Micaiah says "what Yahweh says to me, that I will speak". Chronicles has "what my God says". The oath itself, "as Yahweh lives", is the same. Calling Yahweh "my God" stresses whose prophet Micaiah is.

decisions.choice: as Yahweh lives: an oath
decisions.reason: Micaiah binds himself by an oath in Yahweh's name, the strongest form of promise. He will not shape his message to please the king.

decisions.choice: what my God says, that I will speak: the mark of a true prophet
decisions.reason: A prophet of Yahweh speaks only the words Yahweh gives him (Numbers 22:38; Deuteronomy 18:18). Micaiah's oath sets him apart from prophets who say what the king wants to hear.

decisions.choice: I promise
decisions.reason: Readable adds "I promise" to show that "as surely as the LORD lives" is an oath (m2).

records.source: וַיָּבֹא֮ אֶל־הַמֶּלֶךְ֒ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ אֵלָ֗יו מִיכָה֙ הֲנֵלֵ֞ךְ אֶל־רָמֹ֥ת גִּלְעָ֛ד לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה אִם־אֶחְדָּ֑ל וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ עֲל֣וּ וְהַצְלִ֔יחוּ וְיִנָּתְנ֖וּ בְּיֶדְכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And he came to the king, and said the king to him, Micah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead for battle, or shall I refrain? And he said, go up and succeed, and they will be given into your hand.
pieces: When he came to the king, the king asked him, "Micaiah, shall we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I hold back?" He answered, "Go up and be victorious. They will be given into your hand."

L.14: And he came to the king, and the king said to him, "Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead for battle, or shall I refrain?" And he said, "Go up and succeed, and they will be given into your hand."

R.14: When Micaiah came, the king said, "Micaiah, should we march on Ramoth-gilead, or not?" Micaiah answered, "Attack and win the battle! Your enemies will be handed over to you."

decisions.choice: Micaiah's answer differs in its last words from 1 Kings 22:15
decisions.reason: Here the king calls the prophet by the short form of his name, Micah (the same name), and asks "or shall I refrain?" where Kings has "shall we refrain?". Micaiah's answer is addressed to more than one person ("go up" and "succeed" are plural), and it ends "and they will be given into your hand", where 1 Kings 22:15 has "and Yahweh will give it into the hand of the king".

decisions.choice: go up and succeed: the other prophets' words repeated, not Micaiah's real message
decisions.reason: Micaiah answers with the words of the four hundred (verse 11). The king's reply in verse 15 shows that he heard them as mockery, or at least knew they were not what Micaiah had received from Yahweh. Micaiah gives his true message in verse 16.

decisions.choice: plural: Micaiah speaks to both kings; "they" are the enemy
decisions.reason: The commands and "your" are plural: Micaiah answers both kings. "They will be given" has no stated subject; it most likely means the Arameans, or the people of Ramoth-gilead, delivered into the kings' power.

decisions.choice: shall we go ... or shall I refrain?: the king includes Jehoshaphat, then speaks for himself
decisions.reason: As in verse 5, the king first says "we", including Jehoshaphat, then "I".

decisions.choice: Your enemies will be handed over to you
decisions.reason: Readable names who "they" are (m3), which the context suggests but does not state.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ עַד־כַּמֶּ֥ה פְעָמִ֖ים אֲנִ֣י מַשְׁבִּיעֶ֑ךָ אֲ֠שֶׁר לֹֽא־תְדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלַ֛י רַק־אֱמֶ֖ת בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said to him the king, until how many times [am] I making you swear that not you will speak to me only truth in [the] name of Yahweh?
pieces: But the king said to him, "How often must I put you under oath to tell me only the truth in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"

L.15: And the king said to him, "How many times must I make you swear that you will speak to me nothing but truth in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"

R.15: But the king said to him, "How often must I say this? Swear in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that you will tell me only the truth!"

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:16
decisions.reason: The verse matches 1 Kings 22:16 except for a small difference in the form of one verb, and its wording here is the same.

decisions.choice: how many times must I make you swear?: an angry demand, not a real question
decisions.reason: The king is not counting. He is irritated that Micaiah is not giving him Yahweh's real answer, which suggests he knows the earlier answer was not it, and he puts him under oath.

decisions.choice: in the name of Yahweh: speaking as Yahweh's spokesman
decisions.reason: To speak in Yahweh's name is to speak with his authority, as his messenger (Deuteronomy 18:20-22).

decisions.choice: How many times do I have to tell you? Swear ...
decisions.reason: Readable splits the angry question into a question and a command, keeping its force.

records.source: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר רָאִ֤יתִי אֶת־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ נְפוֹצִ֣ים עַל־הֶֽהָרִ֔ים כַּצֹּ֕אן אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֵין־לָהֶ֖ן רֹעֶ֑ה וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ לֹֽא־אֲדֹנִ֣ים לָאֵ֔לֶּה יָשׁ֥וּבוּ אִישׁ־לְבֵית֖וֹ בְּשָׁלֽוֹם׃
records.gloss: And he said, I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains like the flock which there is not to them a shepherd; and said Yahweh, not masters to these; let them return each to his house in peace.
pieces: Then Micaiah said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the hills, \q like sheep that have no shepherd. \q And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'These have no master; \q let each of them go home in peace.'"

L.16: And he said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, \q like sheep that have no shepherd. \q And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'These have no master; \q let them return each to his house in peace.'"

R.16: Then Micaiah said, "I saw the whole army of Israel scattered over the hills, \q like sheep without anyone to shepherd them. \q And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'These men have no master now. \q Let each of them go home in peace.'"

decisions.choice: the same vision as 1 Kings 22:17
decisions.reason: The verse matches 1 Kings 22:17, with only small differences of spelling, and the wording here is the same, set in the same lines.

decisions.choice: like sheep that have no shepherd: a people whose king is gone
decisions.reason: A king was the shepherd of his people. Moses asked Yahweh for a leader so that his people would not be "like sheep that have no shepherd" (Numbers 27:17). Micaiah sees Israel's army scattered after the battle, leaderless: the king will die.

decisions.choice: these have no master; let them return in peace: the soldiers go home unharmed, without their king
decisions.reason: "Master" (literally "masters", a plural used for one lord) here is the king. The army will not be destroyed; it will go home, but without him (1 Kings 22:36).

decisions.choice: a vision set as a short poem
decisions.reason: Micaiah reports what he saw and heard in two balanced pairs of lines, the form prophets often used for their messages.

decisions.choice: all Israel: Israel's army in the field
decisions.reason: The scattered flock is the army Ahab leads to Ramoth-gilead.

decisions.choice: the whole army of Israel / These men ... now
decisions.reason: Readable makes explicit that the vision is of the army (m5) and that "no master" refers to what will happen after the battle (m3).

records.source: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֶל־יְהוֹשָׁפָ֑ט הֲלֹא֙ אָמַ֣רְתִּי אֵלֶ֔יךָ לֹא־יִתְנַבֵּ֥א עָלַ֛י ט֖וֹב כִּ֥י אִם־לְרָֽע׃ס
records.gloss: And said [the] king of Israel to Jehoshaphat, did not I say to you, not he prophesies concerning me good but only for evil?
pieces: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not say to you that he prophesies nothing good about me, only bad?"

L.17: And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not say to you, 'He does not prophesy good concerning me, but only evil'?"

R.17: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I told you so! He never says anything good about me. He only predicts trouble."

decisions.choice: "but only evil": the same complaint as 1 Kings 22:18
decisions.reason: Chronicles reads "but only for evil" where Kings has "but evil". The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: did I not say to you?: "I told you"
decisions.reason: The question expects agreement. The king turns Micaiah's warning into proof of personal hostility (verse 7) instead of hearing it as Yahweh's word.

decisions.choice: I told you so!
decisions.reason: Readable states as a fact what the king asks as a question (m2). "Bad" and "trouble" as in verse 7.

records.source: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לָכֵ֖ן שִׁמְע֣וּ דְבַר־יְהוָ֑ה רָאִ֤יתִי אֶת־יְהוָה֙ יוֹשֵׁ֣ב עַל־כִּסְא֔וֹ וְכָל־צְבָ֤א הַשָּׁמַ֨יִם֙ עֹֽמְדִ֔ים עַל־יְמִינ֖וֹ וּשְׂמֹאלֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And he said, therefore hear [the] word of Yahweh: I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne, and all [the] host of the heavens standing on his right and his left.
pieces: Micaiah went on, "Then hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I saw {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} seated on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} throne, with all the host of heaven standing at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right and at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.

L.18: And he said, "Therefore hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: I saw {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sitting on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} throne, and all the host of heaven standing on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.

R.18: Micaiah said, "Then listen to what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says. I saw {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sitting on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} throne. All the armies of heaven were standing on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right side and on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.

decisions.choice: small differences from 1 Kings 22:19
decisions.reason: Chronicles has "hear" in the plural, addressed to both kings, and says the host stood "on his right and his left", where Kings has "standing by him, on his right and on his left". The vision is the same.

decisions.choice: I saw Yahweh on his throne: a vision of Yahweh's heavenly court
decisions.reason: Micaiah tells of a vision in which he saw Yahweh as a king holding court, surrounded by his attendants. Isaiah saw Yahweh on his throne in a similar way (Isaiah 6:1-8), and Job 1:6 and 2:1 describe heavenly beings presenting themselves before Yahweh. Micaiah claims to have stood in that council (compare Jeremiah 23:18, 22), unlike the other prophets.

decisions.choice: the host of heaven: the heavenly beings who serve Yahweh
decisions.reason: "Host" means an army. Here the host of heaven is Yahweh's company of heavenly attendants, gathered around his throne like the officials of a royal court. Elsewhere the same phrase can mean the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19).

decisions.choice: therefore: because you will not listen, hear what I saw
decisions.reason: Micaiah answers the king's charge of hostility (verse 17) by explaining where his message came from.

decisions.choice: all the armies of heaven
decisions.reason: Readable says "armies" for "host", the same word used in the title "the LORD of Armies" in these books (m3).

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֗ה מִ֤י יְפַתֶּה֙ אֶת־אַחְאָ֣ב מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְיַ֕עַל וְיִפֹּ֖ל בְּרָמ֣וֹת גִּלְעָ֑ד וַיֹּ֕אמֶר זֶ֚ה אֹמֵ֣ר כָּ֔כָה וְזֶ֖ה אֹמֵ֥ר כָּֽכָה׃
records.gloss: And said Yahweh, who will entice Ahab king of Israel, and he will go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead? And said this [one], saying thus, and this [one] saying thus.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'Who will entice Ahab king of Israel to go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' Some suggested one thing and some another.

L.19: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'Who will entice Ahab king of Israel, so that he goes up and falls at Ramoth-gilead?' And one spoke, saying one thing, and another was saying another.

R.19: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} asked, 'Who will trick Ahab king of Israel into attacking Ramoth-gilead, so that he will die there?' One of them suggested one thing, and another suggested something else.

decisions.choice: "Ahab king of Israel" where 1 Kings 22:20 has "Ahab"
decisions.reason: Chronicles gives Ahab his title, and it words the council's answers a little differently ("one said, saying thus, and another saying thus"). The sense is the same as in 1 Kings 22:20.

decisions.choice: entice: lure, persuade by deceiving
decisions.reason: The verb means to persuade someone, often by deception, to do what will harm him (Judges 14:15; 16:5; Jeremiah 20:7). It is used again in verses 20-21.

decisions.choice: fall: die in battle
decisions.reason: To fall at a place is to be killed there in battle.

decisions.choice: trick ... into attacking ... so that he will die there
decisions.reason: Readable says "trick" for "entice" (m2) and says plainly what "go up and fall" means (m3).

records.source: וַיֵּצֵ֣א הָר֗וּחַ וַֽיַּעֲמֹד֙ לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אֲנִ֣י אֲפַתֶּ֑נּוּ וַיֹּ֧אמֶר יְהוָ֛ה אֵלָ֖יו בַּמָּֽה׃
records.gloss: And came out the spirit and stood before Yahweh, and said, I will entice him. And said Yahweh to him, by what?
pieces: Then a spirit came forward and stood before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, 'I will entice him.' {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} asked him, 'How?'

L.20: And the spirit came out and stood before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, 'I will entice him.' And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, 'By what [means]?'

R.20: Then a spirit came forward and stood in front of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. The spirit said, 'I will trick him.' {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} asked, 'How will you do it?'

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:21
decisions.reason: This verse is word for word the same as 1 Kings 22:21, and its wording here is the same. Unlike there, where many Bibles begin a new verse with the question "By what?", the verse numbering here is the same in the Hebrew text and in other Bibles.

decisions.choice: the spirit: one of the heavenly beings in Yahweh's court
alternatives: a spirit known for this task
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "the spirit", with "the". It may mean simply the particular spirit who stepped forward from the host of verse 18, or a spirit known for this work, or the spirit that moves prophets to speak (compare verse 23). It is not identified further. Spirits sent by God on a task of judgment appear also in Judges 9:23 and 1 Samuel 16:14.

decisions.choice: a spirit
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "a spirit": in English "the spirit" here would suggest a spirit already mentioned or the Spirit of God, and none has been named. Literal keeps the Hebrew "the" (m2).

records.source: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אֵצֵא֙ וְהָיִ֨יתִי֙ לְר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר בְּפִ֖י כָּל־נְבִיאָ֑יו וַיֹּ֗אמֶר תְּפַתֶּה֙ וְגַם־תּוּכָ֔ל צֵ֖א וַעֲשֵׂה־כֵֽן׃
records.gloss: And he said, I will go out and I will be as a spirit of falsehood in [the] mouth of all his prophets. And he said, you will entice and also you will prevail; go out and do so.
pieces: He said, 'I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'You will entice him, and you will succeed. Go and do it.'

L.21: And he said, 'I will go out, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, 'You will entice [him], and you will also succeed; go out and do so.'

R.21: The spirit said, 'I will go out and make all of Ahab's prophets tell lies.' {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'You will trick him, and you will succeed. Go and do it.'

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:22
decisions.reason: The verse matches 1 Kings 22:22. Chronicles adds a small word before "spirit" ("I will become a lying spirit"), which does not change the sense; the wording is the same.

decisions.choice: a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets: Yahweh lets a spirit deceive Ahab's prophets, as judgment on Ahab
alternatives: Yahweh actively sends the deceiving spirit
Yahweh permits a deception Ahab has chosen
the council scene is a vision-picture of Yahweh's judgment
decisions.reason: In Micaiah's vision Yahweh himself asks who will lure Ahab to his death, and he sends the spirit who offers to make Ahab's prophets lie. The passage presents this as Yahweh's judgment on Ahab, which Kings says was already announced for his murder of Naboth (1 Kings 21:19-24). Ahab had long preferred prophets who told him what he wanted to hear (verse 7), and the deception confirms the choice he had made. Yet by telling Ahab the whole vision, Yahweh, through Micaiah, warns him plainly and leaves him free to stay home (verses 22, 27). Scripture elsewhere says that God does not lie (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29), and it speaks of God sending deception on those who refuse the truth (Ezekiel 14:9; 2 Thessalonians 2:11). Whether Micaiah's account is a literal report of a heavenly scene or a vision cast in the picture of a royal council is not stated.

decisions.choice: a spirit of falsehood: a lying spirit
decisions.reason: "Falsehood" describes what the spirit produces: the prophets' words will be false. The phrase is repeated in verse 22.

decisions.choice: you will entice and also prevail: Yahweh's permission and promise of success
decisions.reason: Yahweh's reply grants the spirit's proposal and declares it will work, then sends it out.

decisions.choice: [him] / him
decisions.reason: English needs an object for "entice"; Literal brackets it.

decisions.choice: make all of Ahab's prophets tell lies
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "a lying spirit in the mouth of" the prophets means.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֗ה הִנֵּ֨ה נָתַ֤ן יְהוָה֙ ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר בְּפִ֖י נְבִיאֶ֣יךָ אֵ֑לֶּה וַֽיהוָ֔ה דִּבֶּ֥ר עָלֶ֖יךָ רָעָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And now, look, has put Yahweh a spirit of falsehood in [the] mouth of your prophets these, and Yahweh has spoken concerning you evil.
pieces: So now, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these prophets of yours. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has decreed disaster for you."

L.22: And now, look, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has spoken evil concerning you."

R.22: So you see, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has made these prophets of yours tell lies. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has decided that disaster will come to you."

decisions.choice: "these your prophets" where 1 Kings 22:23 has "all these your prophets"
decisions.reason: Chronicles lacks "all". The sense is the same: the four hundred are meant.

decisions.choice: Yahweh has put a lying spirit in their mouths: the vision applied to Ahab
decisions.reason: Micaiah draws the conclusion of the vision: the unanimous voice of the four hundred is not evidence of truth but the very deception Yahweh allowed (see verse 21). In telling Ahab this, Micaiah gives him the truth the other prophets withheld.

decisions.choice: spoken evil concerning you: announced disaster for you
decisions.reason: "Evil" here, as in verses 7 and 17, is harm or calamity, not wrongdoing. When Yahweh speaks it, it is decreed.

decisions.choice: decreed / decided
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable express that Yahweh's spoken word settles what will happen (m3).

records.source: וַיִּגַּשׁ֙ צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ בֶֽן־כְּנַעֲנָ֔ה וַיַּ֥ךְ אֶת־מִיכָ֖יְהוּ עַל־הַלֶּ֑חִי וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אֵ֣י זֶ֤ה הַדֶּ֨רֶךְ֙ עָבַ֧ר רֽוּחַ־יְהוָ֛ה מֵאִתִּ֖י לְדַבֵּ֥ר אֹתָֽךְ׃
records.gloss: And came near Zedekiah son of Chenaanah and struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said, which [is] this the way [that] passed [the] Spirit of Yahweh from with me to speak with you?
pieces: Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came up and slapped Micaiah on the cheek. "Which way did the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} take from me to speak to you?" he asked.

L.23: And Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "Which way did the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} pass from me to speak with you?"

R.23: Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah walked up to Micaiah and slapped him across the face. He said, "Do you really think the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} left me and went to speak to you?"

decisions.choice: "which is this, the way": a fuller form of the question in 1 Kings 22:24
decisions.reason: Chronicles adds "the way" to Zedekiah's question ("which is the way the Spirit of Yahweh passed ...?"), spelling out what Kings implies. The sense is the same, and so is the wording here.

decisions.choice: struck on the cheek: a public insult
decisions.reason: A slap on the cheek was an act of contempt and humiliation more than an attack to injure (Job 16:10; Lamentations 3:30; Micah 5:1).

decisions.choice: which way did the Spirit pass from me?: a mocking question
decisions.reason: Zedekiah claims that Yahweh's Spirit spoke through him, and scorns the idea that the Spirit could have left him to give Micaiah a different message. His words also echo Micaiah's vision, in which a spirit went out to speak through the prophets (verses 20-22).

decisions.choice: the Spirit of Yahweh: the power by which a prophet speaks
decisions.reason: Prophets spoke when Yahweh's Spirit came on them (Numbers 11:25-29; 1 Samuel 10:6, 10). Zedekiah claims this Spirit; Micaiah's vision has just told the king that a lying spirit was at work in these prophets.

decisions.choice: Do you really think ...?
decisions.reason: Readable brings out the scorn of the question (m3) instead of the "which way" pattern, which is hard to follow in plain English.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מִיכָ֔יְהוּ הִנְּךָ֥ רֹאֶ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא אֲשֶׁ֥ר תָּב֛וֹא חֶ֥דֶר בְּחֶ֖דֶר לְהֵחָבֵֽא׃
records.gloss: And said Micaiah, look, you [are] seeing on that day when you go [into a] room within [a] room to hide yourself.
pieces: Micaiah replied, "You will find out on the day you go into an inner room to hide."

L.24: And Micaiah said, "Look, you will see on that day when you go into an inner room to hide yourself."

R.24: Micaiah answered, "You will find out on the day you run into a back room to hide."

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:25
decisions.reason: The verse matches 1 Kings 22:25 except for small differences of spelling, and its wording here is the same.

decisions.choice: a room within a room: an inner room
decisions.reason: The phrase means a room deep inside a house, where someone could hide (1 Kings 20:30).

decisions.choice: you will see: you will find out who spoke truly
decisions.reason: Micaiah answers Zedekiah's question by pointing to the day his prophecy is proved false and he has to hide for his life, perhaps when the defeat is known or when the king's successor deals with the prophets who misled him. The text does not tell what happened to Zedekiah.

decisions.choice: find out
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "find out" for "see", the sense here (m3).

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל קְחוּ֙ אֶת־מִיכָ֔יְהוּ וַהֲשִׁיבֻ֖הוּ אֶל־אָמ֣וֹן שַׂר־הָעִ֑יר וְאֶל־יוֹאָ֖שׁ בֶּן־הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And said [the] king of Israel, take Micaiah and return him to Amon [the] governor of the city and to Joash son of the king,
pieces: Then the king of Israel ordered, "Take Micaiah and send him back to Amon, the city governor, and to Joash, the king's son,

L.25: And the king of Israel said, "Take Micaiah and return him to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son,

R.25: Then the king of Israel said, "Arrest Micaiah! Take him back to Amon, who governs the city, and to Joash, the king's son.

decisions.choice: the same order as 1 Kings 22:26
decisions.reason: The verse matches 1 Kings 22:26 except for small differences in the form of two verbs, and its wording here is the same.

decisions.choice: return him: send him back to those who had kept him
decisions.reason: "Return" suggests that Micaiah had been in the keeping of these officials before he was called, perhaps already under arrest.

decisions.choice: the official of the city: the governor of Samaria
decisions.reason: The word for an official or commander, with "of the city", names the officer in charge of the capital (2 Kings 23:8).

decisions.choice: the king's son: a royal son, or a title of a royal officer
decisions.reason: Joash may have been one of Ahab's sons. "The king's son" may also be the title of an officer who guarded prisoners (Jeremiah 36:26; 38:6).

decisions.choice: governor
decisions.reason: Every level says "governor", the clearest English for the officer in charge of a city (m3), rather than "prince" or "official".

records.source: וַאֲמַרְתֶּ֗ם כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ שִׂ֥ימוּ זֶ֖ה בֵּ֣ית הַכֶּ֑לֶא וְהַאֲכִלֻ֜הוּ לֶ֤חֶם לַ֨חַץ֙ וּמַ֣יִם לַ֔חַץ עַ֖ד שׁוּבִ֥י בְשָׁלֽוֹם׃
records.gloss: and you shall say, thus says the king, put this [one in the] house of the prison, and feed him bread of oppression and water of oppression until I return in peace.
pieces: and tell them, 'The king says this: "Put this man in prison and feed him with scant bread and scant water until I come back safely."'"

L.26: and say, 'Thus says the king: "Put this [man] in the prison house, and feed him bread of affliction and water of affliction until I return in peace."'"

R.26: Tell them the king says to put this man in prison. Give him only a little bread and water until I come back safely."

decisions.choice: "until I return in peace" where 1 Kings 22:27 has "until I come in peace"
decisions.reason: Chronicles uses the verb "return", the same verb Micaiah takes up in his reply ("if you indeed return in peace", verse 27). Otherwise the order is the same as in 1 Kings 22:27.

decisions.choice: bread of oppression and water of oppression: the meager rations of a prisoner
decisions.reason: "Oppression" describes hardship. The phrase means bare, reduced rations of bread and water (compare Isaiah 30:20).

decisions.choice: until I return in peace: until I come back safely
decisions.reason: The king assumes he will come back unharmed, which is exactly what Micaiah has denied. Micaiah takes up the words in verse 27.

decisions.choice: scant bread and scant water
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the two parallel phrases while saying what they mean (m2).

decisions.choice: indirect speech
decisions.reason: Readable turns the message inside the order into indirect speech, to avoid quotation marks three deep.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מִיכָ֔יְהוּ אִם־שׁ֤וֹב תָּשׁוּב֙ בְּשָׁל֔וֹם לֹא־דִבֶּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה בִּ֑י וַיֹּ֕אמֶר שִׁמְע֖וּ עַמִּ֥ים כֻּלָּֽם׃פ
records.gloss: And said Micaiah, if returning you return in peace, not has spoken Yahweh by me. And he said, hear, peoples, all of them.
pieces: Micaiah said, "If you ever come back safely, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has not spoken through me." And he added, "Listen, all you peoples!"

L.27: And Micaiah said, "If you indeed return in peace, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has not spoken by me." And he said, "Hear, peoples, all of them."

R.27: Micaiah said, "If you ever come back safely, then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has not spoken through me." Then he said to everyone there, "Remember what I have said!"

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:28
decisions.reason: This verse is word for word the same as 1 Kings 22:28, and its wording here is the same.

decisions.choice: if you return in peace, Yahweh has not spoken by me: the test of a prophet
decisions.reason: The law gave this test: a prophecy that does not come true was not spoken by Yahweh (Deuteronomy 18:21-22). Micaiah stakes his standing as a prophet on the king's death.

decisions.choice: hear, peoples, all of them: the opening words of the book of Micah
decisions.reason: The same words begin the prophecy of Micah (Micah 1:2). Here they call everyone present to witness what Micaiah has said. The phrase is missing from the main ancient Greek translation of 1 Kings 22:28, and some think it was added there by a copier who linked Micaiah with the later prophet Micah; it is in the Hebrew text of both Kings and Chronicles.

decisions.choice: peoples: everyone present, or the nations
decisions.reason: "Peoples" usually means nations. Here it is a call to all who hear, to bear witness.

decisions.choice: he said to everyone there, "Remember what I have said!"
decisions.reason: Readable says what the call is for (m3, m4): those present are to witness the prophecy.

records.source: וַיַּ֧עַל מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל וִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֖ה אֶל־רָמֹ֥ת גִּלְעָֽד׃
records.gloss: And went up [the] king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah to Ramoth-gilead.
pieces: So the king of Israel went up to Ramoth-gilead, and Jehoshaphat king of Judah with him.

L.28: And the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.

R.28: So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went to attack Ramoth-gilead.

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:29, with "to"
decisions.reason: Chronicles adds the word "to" before Ramoth-gilead, which Kings leaves to be understood. The sense is the same as in 1 Kings 22:29.

decisions.choice: went up: marched to battle
decisions.reason: "Go up" was the word of the prophets' promise (verses 5, 11, 14) and of Yahweh's question (verse 19). The king does what the deception was meant to make him do.

decisions.choice: went to attack
decisions.reason: Readable says what "went up" means here (m2).

records.heading: Ahab dies at Ramoth-gilead

records.source: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל אֶל־יְהוֹשָׁפָ֗ט הִתְחַפֵּשׂ֙ וָב֣וֹא בַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וְאַתָּ֖ה לְבַ֣שׁ בְּגָדֶ֑יךָ וַיִּתְחַפֵּשׂ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said [the] king of Israel to Jehoshaphat, disguising myself and going into the battle, and you, wear your garments. And disguised himself [the] king of Israel, and they went into the battle.
pieces: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will go into the battle in disguise, but you should put on your royal robes." So the king of Israel disguised himself, and the two of them went into the fight.

L.29: And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "[I will] disguise myself and go into the battle, but you, put on your robes." And the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into the battle.

R.29: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will dress like an ordinary soldier when I go into battle, but you should wear your royal robes." So the king of Israel put on a disguise, and the two kings went to fight.

decisions.choice: "they went" where 1 Kings 22:30 has "he went"
decisions.reason: In Kings the king of Israel disguises himself and goes into the battle. Chronicles has the plural, "and they went into the battle": both kings went. Otherwise the verse is the same as 1 Kings 22:30.

decisions.choice: disguising myself and going: an infinitive used as a statement of intention
decisions.reason: The Hebrew uses two infinitives, a short, clipped way of saying "I will disguise myself and go".

decisions.choice: the king's disguise: an attempt to escape the prophecy
decisions.reason: Ahab tries to make himself unrecognizable so that he cannot be singled out, perhaps having heard of the Aramean order (verse 30) or fearing Micaiah's word. Jehoshaphat, in royal robes, becomes the obvious target (verse 31). Saul too disguised himself before his final battle (1 Samuel 28:8), and Josiah would later do the same (35:22).

decisions.choice: dress like an ordinary soldier
decisions.reason: Readable says what the disguise was for, the first time; it then uses "disguised".

decisions.choice: the two of them / the two kings
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that "they" are both kings (m1).

records.source: וּמֶ֣לֶךְ אֲרָ֡ם צִוָּה֩ אֶת־שָׂרֵ֨י הָרֶ֤כֶב אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר לֹ֚א תִּלָּ֣חֲמ֔וּ אֶת־הַקָּטֹ֖ן אֶת־הַגָּד֑וֹל כִּ֛י אִֽם־אֶת־מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְבַדּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And [the] king of Aram had commanded [the] commanders of the chariotry that [were] his, saying, not you shall fight with the small, with the great, but with [the] king of Israel by himself.
pieces: Now the king of Aram had given an order to his chariot commanders: "Fight with no one, small or great, but the king of Israel alone."

L.30: And the king of Aram had commanded the commanders of the chariots that [were] his, saying, "Do not fight with the small [or] the great, but only with the king of Israel alone."

R.30: The king of Aram had given orders to his chariot commanders: "Do not attack anyone except the king of Israel."

decisions.choice: no number of commanders, where 1 Kings 22:31 has "thirty-two"
decisions.reason: Chronicles does not give the number of the chariot commanders, which Kings links to the thirty-two kings of 1 Kings 20:1, 24. It also says "with the small, with the great" without "or". The order is the same as in 1 Kings 22:31.

decisions.choice: small and great: anyone at all
decisions.reason: Naming the two extremes means everyone. The Aramean chariots are to ignore every other soldier and hunt down the king.

decisions.choice: the king of Israel alone: the target is the king
decisions.reason: Killing the enemy king would end the battle. The order explains Ahab's disguise and the danger to Jehoshaphat in his royal robes.

decisions.choice: [or]
decisions.reason: Literal brackets "or", which English needs between the two words. Readable drops the pair "small or great" and says "anyone" (m2).

records.source: וַיְהִ֡י כִּרְאוֹת֩ שָׂרֵ֨י הָרֶ֜כֶב אֶת־יְהוֹשָׁפָ֗ט וְהֵ֤מָּה אָֽמְרוּ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל ה֔וּא וַיָּסֹ֥בּוּ עָלָ֖יו לְהִלָּחֵ֑ם וַיִּזְעַ֤ק יְהֽוֹשָׁפָט֙ וַֽיהוָ֣ה עֲזָר֔וֹ וַיְסִיתֵ֥ם אֱלֹהִ֖ים מִמֶּֽנּוּ׃
records.gloss: And it was, when saw [the] commanders of the chariotry Jehoshaphat, and they said, [the] king of Israel [is] he; and they surrounded him to fight, and cried out Jehoshaphat, and Yahweh helped him, and enticed them God away from him.
pieces: When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "That is the king of Israel!" So they closed in on him to attack, and Jehoshaphat cried out. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} helped him; God drew them away from him.

L.31: And it happened, when the commanders of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, that they said, "He [is] the king of Israel." And they surrounded him to fight, and Jehoshaphat cried out, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} helped him, and God drew them away from him.

R.31: When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat in his royal robes, they said, "That is the king of Israel!" So they surrounded him to attack him. But Jehoshaphat cried out, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} helped him. God made them turn away from him.

decisions.choice: "and Yahweh helped him; God drew them away from him", added to 1 Kings 22:32
decisions.reason: Kings tells only that Jehoshaphat cried out; the next verse tells that the commanders turned back when they saw he was not the king of Israel. Chronicles adds that Yahweh helped him and that God drew the attackers away, so Jehoshaphat's cry is a cry to Yahweh and his escape is Yahweh's answer. Chronicles also lacks "surely" ("surely he is the king of Israel") and says the commanders "surrounded" him where Kings says they "turned aside" against him.

decisions.choice: cried out ... Yahweh helped him: the God who answers those who call on him
decisions.reason: Chronicles often tells how those who cried to Yahweh in battle were heard and helped (1 Chronicles 5:20; 2 Chronicles 13:14-15; 14:10). Jehoshaphat had joined Ahab's war, but in his danger he called on Yahweh and was saved.

decisions.choice: drew them away: the same verb as "enticed" in verse 2
decisions.reason: The verb means to urge or lure. In verse 2 Ahab lured Jehoshaphat into the war; here God lures the enemy chariots away from him.

decisions.choice: surrounded: closed in on him
decisions.reason: The verb means to turn or go around; with "against" it describes the chariots wheeling round to close in on Jehoshaphat.

decisions.choice: in his royal robes
decisions.reason: Readable reminds the reader why they took him for the king (verse 29), as in 1 Kings 22:32.

decisions.choice: made them turn away
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what God's luring them away meant (m3): the commanders turned away from Jehoshaphat.

records.source: וַיְהִ֗י כִּרְאוֹת֙ שָׂרֵ֣י הָרֶ֔כֶב כִּ֥י לֹא־הָיָ֖ה מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיָּשֻׁ֖בוּ מֵאַחֲרָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And it was, when saw [the] commanders of the chariotry that not was [it the] king of Israel, and they turned back from after him.
pieces: Once the chariot commanders saw he was not Israel's king, they broke off the chase.

L.32: And it happened, when the commanders of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, that they turned back from pursuing him.

R.32: When the chariot commanders realized he was not the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him.

decisions.choice: the same words as 1 Kings 22:33
decisions.reason: Chronicles says "that it was not the king of Israel" where Kings says "that he was not the king of Israel"; the sense is the same. In Chronicles this follows God's drawing them away (verse 31).

decisions.choice: turned back from after him: stopped pursuing him
decisions.reason: "From after him" means from following him; the commanders broke off the chase, as their orders required (verse 30).

decisions.choice: realized
decisions.reason: Readable says "realized" for "saw", since they understood rather than looked.

records.source: וְאִ֗ישׁ מָשַׁ֤ךְ בַּקֶּ֨שֶׁת֙ לְתֻמּ֔וֹ וַיַּךְ֙ אֶת־מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בֵּ֥ין הַדְּבָקִ֖ים וּבֵ֣ין הַשִּׁרְיָ֑ן וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָֽרַכָּ֗ב הֲפֹ֧ךְ יָדְךָ֛ וְהוֹצֵאתַ֥נִי מִן־הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֖ה כִּ֥י הָחֳלֵֽיתִי׃
records.gloss: And a man drew on the bow in his innocence and struck [the] king of Israel between the scales and between the armor; and he said to the chariot driver, turn your hand and bring me out from the camp, for I am wounded.
pieces: But a man drew his bow at random and hit the king of Israel between the joints of his scale armor and the breastplate. The king said to the chariot driver, "Turn around and get me out of the battle, because I am wounded."

L.33: And a man drew the bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the joints of the armor and the breastplate. And he said to the chariot driver, "Turn your hand and take me out of the camp, for I am wounded."

R.33: But an Aramean soldier shot an arrow without aiming at anyone in particular. It hit the king of Israel where his armor joined together. The king said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and take me away from the fighting! I am wounded."

decisions.choice: the same account as 1 Kings 22:34
decisions.reason: The verse matches 1 Kings 22:34. Chronicles says "the chariot driver" where Kings says "his chariot driver", and has "your hand" in a slightly different form; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: in his innocence: at random, without aiming at the king
decisions.reason: The word means simplicity or innocence. The archer shot without a particular target and with no idea who he hit. What the Aramean commanders failed to do with their orders, one unaimed arrow did, as Micaiah had said.

decisions.choice: between the scales and the armor: at a gap where pieces of armor met
alternatives: between the joints and the coat of mail
between the lower armor and the breastplate
decisions.reason: The two words are rare and their exact meaning is not certain. The first, from a root meaning "to cling, to join", may name the joints or the small overlapping plates of scale armor; the second names a coat of mail or breastplate. The arrow struck at a weak point where they met, perhaps under the arm or at the waist.

decisions.choice: turn your hand: turn the chariot around
decisions.reason: The driver holds the reins in his hand; to turn his hand is to turn the horses.

decisions.choice: the camp: the army, the battle lines
decisions.reason: Here "camp" means the army drawn up in battle, so to be taken out of it is to leave the fighting.

decisions.choice: an Aramean soldier
decisions.reason: Readable says that the archer was one of the enemy, which the context makes plain.

decisions.choice: joints ... breastplate / where his armor joined together
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced name the two parts of the armor; Readable gives the sense that matters, a gap in the armor (m3).

records.gloss: And went up the battle on that day, and [the] king of Israel was holding [himself] upright in the chariot opposite Aram until the evening; and he died at [the] time of [the] going of the sun.
pieces: All that day the battle grew fiercer, and the king of Israel kept himself upright in his chariot facing the Arameans until evening. At sunset he died.

L.34: And the battle went up on that day, and the king of Israel was holding [himself] upright in the chariot facing Aram until the evening; and he died at the time of the going of the sun.

R.34: The battle grew worse all that day. The king of Israel stayed propped up in his chariot, facing the Arameans, until evening. As the sun went down, he died.

decisions.choice: Ahab's death told more briefly than in 1 Kings 22:35-38
decisions.reason: Kings says the king was propped up in the chariot and died in the evening, and that the blood of his wound ran into the chariot; it goes on to the army sent home, his burial in Samaria, and the dogs licking his blood as Yahweh had said (1 Kings 22:36-38). Chronicles ends with his death at sunset and does not name him again. Its story stays with Jehoshaphat, who returns safely to Jerusalem (19:1).

decisions.choice: was holding himself upright: an active form where Kings has "was propped up"
decisions.reason: Kings uses a passive form ("was made to stand"); Chronicles uses an active one ("was making stand"). It may mean that the king held himself up, or, with no object stated, that someone kept him upright. Either way he stayed upright in the chariot until he died.

decisions.choice: the battle went up: the battle rose, grew fierce
decisions.reason: The fighting increased in intensity through the day.

decisions.choice: upright in the chariot facing Aram: so the troops would not lose heart
decisions.reason: Instead of leaving the field as he had ordered (verse 33), the king stayed upright in his chariot, facing the enemy, perhaps so that his army would not see that he was wounded. He bled to death through the day.

decisions.choice: he died: Micaiah's word fulfilled
decisions.reason: The king does not "return in peace" (verses 26-27). As Micaiah had said, he died at Ramoth-gilead, and the flock was left without its shepherd (verse 16).

decisions.choice: grew fierce / grew worse
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "went up" means here (m3).

decisions.choice: At sunset / As the sun went down
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "the time of the going of the sun" in ordinary words.
